content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has released updated recommendations for the treatment of three major sexually transmitted infections (STIs): Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonorrhea), Chlamydia trachomatis (chlamydia), and Treponema pallidum (syphilis). These updates also include new guidance on syphilis testing and partner services. The recommendations are based on the latest evidence and aim to address the global burden of STIs, which remains high and contributes significantly to morbidity, mortality, and economic costs worldwide. Gonorrhea and chlamydia are the most common bacterial STIs globally, while syphilis, caused by Treponema pallidum, can lead to severe health outcomes, including congenital syphilis, which poses devastating risks to fetuses if not detected and treated early during pregnancy. WHO has set ambitious targets to reduce gonorrhea and syphilis infections by 90% and eliminate congenital syphilis as a public health problem by 2030. Achieving these goals requires improved access to prevention, diagnostic, and treatment services for individuals with STIs. The treatment of STIs is increasingly complicated by the emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). For Neisseria gonorrhoeae, resistance has developed against nearly all antibiotics used for first-line empirical treatment, with ceftriaxone (an extended-spectrum cephalosporin) being the last effective option in many countries. To address this, the updated guidelines recommend increasing the dosage of ceftriaxone to delay resistance development and provide additional treatment options for specific settings. The use of azithromycin, which is highly prone to resistance, is now reserved for certain infections, such as Mycoplasma genitalium. For Chlamydia trachomatis, the updated recommendations emphasize the efficacy of doxycycline as a preferred treatment option. For syphilis, benzathine penicillin remains the most effective treatment, particularly for preventing vertical transmission during pregnancy. The guidelines also highlight the importance of addressing potential allergic reactions to penicillin in patients. In response to the rising number of syphilis cases, WHO has introduced new testing strategies to increase coverage. These include the use of dual treponemal/non-treponemal rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and syphilis self-testing as additional options. These approaches aim to improve early detection and treatment, thereby reducing transmission and reinfection rates. The guidelines also provide evidence-based recommendations to enhance STI partner services. Strategies include patient referral, provider-assisted notification, and expedited partner therapy (EPT), where medication or prescriptions are provided to partners without requiring prior clinical examination. The guidelines are intended to support policymakers, program managers, and healthcare providers in updating national STI guidelines to meet the 2030 global health sector strategy targets. They will also be incorporated into WHO’s forthcoming consolidated guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care of STIs.
